evidence.shows: US 2019: $22.6 billion print vs $2.04 billion e-book revenue.

verdicts.reading: By 2019 the navigation function of these blind-assistance glasses has been perfected.
verdicts.mainstream_test: Event test: reliable, complete navigation guidance from such systems by 2021, late by 2024.
verdicts.reason: The leading eyeglass system (OrCam MyEye) had no navigation function; blind navigation relied on canes, guide dogs and phone GPS apps, and no wearable system offered perfected navigation by 2024.

evidence.title: OrCam (Wikipedia)
evidence.shows: MyEye features are text reading, face and barcode recognition; no navigation capabilities described.

verdicts.reading: These reading-navigation assistants communicate with blind users by speech and by tactile signals.
verdicts.mainstream_test: Capability test on existing systems.
verdicts.reason: Existing eyeglass systems spoke to the user (OrCam audio output), and separate haptic aids existed, but the eyeglass readers themselves did not combine speech with tactile indicators. Partly true.

evidence.title: OrCam (Wikipedia)
evidence.shows: MyEye delivers information as spoken audio to the wearer's ear; no tactile output described.

verdicts.reading: These visual-interpretation systems are also widely used by sighted people to interpret the visual world.
verdicts.mainstream_test: D16 mainstream: at least 20% of sighted users in major markets using machine visual interpretation; form factor (eyeglasses) noted.
verdicts.reason: Machine visual interpretation became widely used by sighted people via phones (Google Lens from October 2017, integrated into Android camera and Google apps), but not through eyeglass-mounted systems as described. The function is mainstream, the device is not. Partial.

evidence.title: Google Lens (Wikipedia)
evidence.shows: Launched Oct 2017; identifies objects, reads text and labels, translates via the phone camera; integrated into Photos, Assistant and the camera.

verdicts.reading: By 2019 retinal and visual neural implants exist but are limited and used by only a small share of blind people.
verdicts.mainstream_test: Event test plus the stated low adoption (the claim predicts a small share).
verdicts.reason: Argus II retinal prosthesis was approved in the EU (2011) and US (2013), restoring limited vision at about $150,000, used by few patients; production stopped in 2020. Exactly the predicted state.

evidence.title: Argus retinal prosthesis (Wikipedia)
evidence.shows: EU approval March 2011, US February 2013 under humanitarian exemption; about $150,000; small trials; production ceased 2020.

verdicts.reading: By 2019 deaf people routinely read others' speech as captions in their eyeglass/lens displays.
verdicts.mainstream_test: D16 mainstream: at least 20% of deaf people routinely using lens-display captioning.
verdicts.reason: Real-time captioning became common on phones (Google Live Transcribe, February 2019), but captioning glasses stayed niche through 2024, since direct-eye displays never spread (see 149). The stated lens-display mode did not reach 5%.

evidence.title: Live Transcribe (Wikipedia)
evidence.shows: Phone-based real-time captioning app for deaf users launched Feb 2019 on Android, not a lens display.

evidence.title: Smart glasses (Wikipedia)
evidence.shows: No mainstream adoption of smart glasses through 2024.

verdicts.reading: By 2019 there are systems that give deaf people visual and tactile renderings of sounds such as music, with debate over whether they match hearing.
verdicts.mainstream_test: Existence test (the claim states existence, not adoption).
verdicts.reason: Sound-to-touch devices for the deaf were on sale: Neosensory's VEST (2015) and Buzz wristband (2019) turn sound into vibration patterns; research notes substituted perception differs from native hearing.

evidence.title: David Eagleman (Wikipedia)
evidence.shows: Neosensory VEST (2015) translates audio into vibrations for deaf users; Buzz wristband (2019) turns sound into vibration patterns.

evidence.title: Sensory substitution (Wikipedia)
evidence.shows: Sound-to-touch hearing devices exist; substituted perception differs by user, the subject of research debate.

verdicts.reading: By 2019 cochlear and other hearing implants are very effective and widely used.
verdicts.mainstream_test: Adoption test: established standard treatment with large user numbers (several hundred thousand) in major markets.
verdicts.reason: About 736,900 cochlear implants had been registered worldwide by December 2019 (US: about 118,100 adults and 65,000 children); they are standard of care for severe-to-profound deafness. Uptake among all eligible adults is lower, but 'widely used' holds.

evidence.title: Cochlear Implants (NIDCD, NIH)
evidence.shows: About 736,900 cochlear implants registered worldwide as of Dec 2019; about 118,100 in US adults and 65,000 in children.

verdicts.reading: By 2019 paraplegics and some quadriplegics routinely walk and climb stairs using computer-controlled nerve stimulation and robotic exoskeletons.
verdicts.mainstream_test: D16 mainstream: at least 20% of paraplegics using such systems routinely; miss below 5%.
verdicts.reason: The first FDA-cleared personal exoskeleton (ReWalk) came in 2014; exoskeletons are costly and used by a small number of people, mostly in rehabilitation clinics. Routine walking by paraplegics did not happen by 2024.

evidence.title: Powered exoskeleton (Wikipedia)
evidence.shows: ReWalk first FDA-approved exoskeleton for paralysed users in 2014; prices up to hundreds of thousands of dollars; no evidence of routine use.

verdicts.reading: By 2019 disabilities such as blindness, deafness and paraplegia are generally unnoticeable and not regarded as significant.
verdicts.mainstream_test: Outcome test: disability no longer a significant disadvantage (for example in employment).
verdicts.reason: In 2019 the US employment-population ratio was 19.3% for people with a disability against 66.3% without, a gap at every age; assistive technology had not made these disabilities insignificant.

evidence.title: Persons with a Disability: Labor Force Characteristics 2019 (BLS)
evidence.shows: Employment-population ratio 19.3% for persons with a disability vs 66.3% without, 2019.

verdicts.reading: By 2019 you can do virtually anything with anyone regardless of distance, using easy, ever-present technology.
verdicts.mainstream_test: D16 mainstream on remote interaction: at least 20% of people routinely using easy remote communication and collaboration.
verdicts.reason: Easy remote communication (video calls, messaging, shared documents, online games) was ubiquitous, and in 2020 Zoom went from 10 million to over 300 million daily meeting participants; but physical activities and touch could not be done remotely. 'Virtually anything' overstates. Partly true.

evidence.title: Zoom (software) (Wikipedia)
evidence.shows: Daily meeting participants rose from 10 million (Dec 2019) to over 300 million joins (April 2020).

verdicts.reading: By 2019 phone calls routinely include high-resolution 3D images projected through direct-eye displays and auditory lenses.
verdicts.mainstream_test: D16 mainstream: at least 20% of calls with 3D eyewear imagery.
verdicts.reason: Video calls were flat 2D on phones and computers; direct-eye displays stayed niche (see 149) and 3D telepresence (for example research prototypes) was not routine by 2024.

evidence.title: Smart glasses (Wikipedia)
evidence.shows: No mainstream adoption of eyewear displays; Google Glass consumer product discontinued 2015.

verdicts.reading: By 2019 three-dimensional holographic displays have emerged (exist as products), as an alternative to eyewear for 3D calls.
verdicts.mainstream_test: Existence test (the claim says 'emerged', not widespread).
verdicts.reason: Commercial glasses-free 'holographic' 3D displays existed: Looking Glass light-field display (Kickstarter July 2018, shipping December 2018, 45 views). They are light-field rather than true holograms and niche, which makes the call uncertain.

evidence.title: The Looking Glass: A Holographic Display for 3D Creators (Kickstarter)
evidence.shows: Desktop holographic (light-field) display, 45 views, from $499, funded Aug 2018, shipping Dec 2018.

evidence.title: Holographic display (Wikipedia)
evidence.shows: Holographic displays predicted to enter mass market within ten years (2013); only niche commercial uses listed.

verdicts.reading: By 2019 people on such 3D calls feel as if they are physically near the other person.
verdicts.mainstream_test: Event test: routine telepresence giving a sense of physical co-presence by 2021, late by 2024.
verdicts.reason: Mainstream calls remained 2D video; the 3D eyewear and holographic call systems presupposed were not in use, and co-presence-grade telepresence stayed in research demos through 2024.

evidence.title: Zoom (software) (Wikipedia)
evidence.shows: The dominant remote-meeting tool was 2D video conferencing.

verdicts.reading: By 2019 the resolution of these 3D call images equals or exceeds optimal human visual acuity.
verdicts.mainstream_test: Capability test on the 3D call imagery (direct-eye or holographic).
verdicts.reason: The 3D call displays (retinal or holographic) did not reach human-acuity resolution: retinal projection products were about 720p and light-field displays far lower per view. Flat phone screens reached high ppi, but that is not the claimed 3D imagery.

evidence.title: Virtual retinal display (Wikipedia)
evidence.shows: RETISSA Display II (2019) resolution about 720p, well below human acuity across the visual field.

verdicts.reading: By 2019 a person can be fooled into thinking a remotely projected person is physically present.
verdicts.mainstream_test: Event test: routinely available telepresence indistinguishable from physical presence by 2021, late by 2024.
verdicts.reason: No available communication system produced projections indistinguishable from a present person by 2024; calls used 2D screens and niche AR headsets.

evidence.title: Holographic display (Wikipedia)
evidence.shows: Holographic displays not in the mass market; only niche implementations.

verdicts.reading: By 2019 most meetings take place without the participants being physically together.
verdicts.mainstream_test: Share test: more than 50% of meetings held remotely.
verdicts.reason: In 2019 remote meetings were a minority (Zoom had at most 10 million daily participants in December 2019); in 2020-21 the pandemic moved most office meetings online (over 300 million daily joins), but only for remote-capable work and partly reversed after 2022. No measure shows a durable majority of all meetings remote. Partly true.

evidence.title: Zoom (software) (Wikipedia)
evidence.shows: 10 million daily meeting participants in Dec 2019, over 200 million in March 2020 and over 300 million joins in April 2020.

verdicts.reading: By 2019 high-quality speech-to-speech translation for most common language pairs is routinely available in communication technology.
verdicts.mainstream_test: Availability test on mass-market devices (routinely available, not routinely used).
verdicts.reason: Google Translate conversation mode on phones (from 2011) and Google Assistant interpreter mode on Android and iOS phones (December 2019, previously on Google Home) provided real-time conversation translation across dozens of languages on mass-market devices. Quality was good, not perfect.

evidence.title: Google Assistant (Wikipedia)
evidence.shows: Interpreter mode in Assistant phone apps for Android and iOS from Dec 2019, translating conversations in real time.

evidence.title: Google Translate (Wikipedia)
evidence.shows: Conversation mode for spoken translation since January 2011.
